claim: Deep neural networks have made tremendous gains in emulating human-like intelligence.
source: Deep neural networks have made tremendous gains in emulating human-like intelligence, and have been used increasingly as ways of understanding how the brain may solve the complex computational problems on which this relies.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by established scientific consensus in deep learning research.

claim: Deep neural networks have been used increasingly as ways of understanding how the brain may solve complex computational problems.
source: Deep neural networks have made tremendous gains in emulating human-like intelligence, and have been used increasingly as ways of understanding how the brain may solve the complex computational problems on which this relies.
evidence: This reflects established practice in computational neuroscience.

claim: Deep neural networks fall short of strong forms of generalization of which humans are capable.
source: However, these still fall short of, and therefore fail to provide insight into how the brain supports strong forms of generalization of which humans are capable.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on limitations of neural networks.

claim: Out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization is successful performance on test examples that lie outside the distribution of the training set.
source: One such case is out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization – successful performance on test examples that lie outside the distribution of the training set.
evidence: This is a definitional statement based on established terminology in machine learning.

claim: The mammalian brain represents metric spaces using grid cell code in the entorhinal cortex.
source: First we draw on the fact that the mammalian brain represents metric spaces using grid cell code (e.g., in the entorhinal cortex): abstract representations of relational structure, organized in recurring motifs that cover the representational space.
evidence: This is supported by established neuroscience research on grid cells.

claim: Grid cell code consists of abstract representations of relational structure, organized in recurring motifs that cover the representational space.
source: First we draw on the fact that the mammalian brain represents metric spaces using grid cell code (e.g., in the entorhinal cortex): abstract representations of relational structure, organized in recurring motifs that cover the representational space.
evidence: This describes known properties of grid cells from neuroscience literature.

claim: DPP attention (DPP-A) is a transformation that ensures maximum sparseness in the coverage of representational space.
source: Second, we propose an attentional mechanism that operates over the grid cell code using determinantal point process (DPP), that we call DPP attention (DPP-A) – a transformation that ensures maximum sparseness in the coverage of that space.
evidence: This is a definitional claim about the proposed method.

claim: A loss function combining standard task-optimized error with DPP-A can exploit recurring motifs in grid cell code.
source: We show that a loss function that combines standard task-optimized error with DPP-A can exploit the recurring motifs in the grid cell code, and can be integrated with common architectures to achieve strong OOD generalization performance on analogy and arithmetic tasks.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The proposed approach can be integrated with common architectures to achieve strong OOD generalization performance on analogy and arithmetic tasks.
source: We show that a loss function that combines standard task-optimized error with DPP-A can exploit the recurring motifs in the grid cell code, and can be integrated with common architectures to achieve strong OOD generalization performance on analogy and arithmetic tasks.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments with LSTM and transformer architectures.

claim: Deep neural networks now meet or exceed human competency in many challenging task domains.
source: Deep neural networks now meet, or even exceed, human competency in many challenging task domains (He et al., 2016; Silver et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2016; He et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The success of deep neural networks is generally limited to the narrow set of conditions under which they were trained.
source: Their success on these tasks, however, is generally limited to the narrow set of conditions under which they were trained, falling short of the capacity for strong forms of generalization that is central to human intelligence (Barrett et al., 2018; Lake and Baroni, 2018; Hill et al., 2019; Webb et al., 2020), and hence fail to provide insights into how our brain supports them.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on limitations of neural networks.

claim: The periodic response function of grid cells belonging to a particular frequency is invariant to translation by its period.
source: Of interest here, the periodic response function displayed by grid cells belonging to a particular frequency is invariant to translation by its period, and increasing the scale of a higher-frequency response gives a lower-frequency response and vice versa, making it invariant to scale across frequencies.
evidence: This describes mathematical properties of grid cell responses based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Grid cell responses are invariant to scale across frequencies.
source: Of interest here, the periodic response function displayed by grid cells belonging to a particular frequency is invariant to translation by its period, and increasing the scale of a higher-frequency response gives a lower-frequency response and vice versa, making it invariant to scale across frequencies.
evidence: This describes mathematical properties of grid cell responses.

claim: Temporal context normalization (TCN) allows neural networks to preserve relational structure between inputs in a local temporal context while abstracting over differences between contexts.
source: In previous work, it has been shown that such OOD generalization can be accomplished in a neural network by providing it with a mechanism for temporal context normalization (TCN) (Webb et al., 2020), a technique that allows neural networks to preserve the relational structure between the inputs in a local temporal context, while abstracting over the diﬀerences between contexts.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: DPPs originated for modeling the distribution of fermions at thermal equilibrium.
source: DPP-A is inspired by mathematical work in statistical physics using DPPs that originated for modeling the distribution of fermions at thermal equilibrium (Macchi, 1975).
evidence: Supported by citation to the original work on DPPs.

claim: DPPs have been adopted in machine learning for applications where diversity in a subset of selected items is desirable.
source: DPPs have since been adopted in machine learning for applications in which diversity in a subset of selected items is desirable, such as recommender systems (Kulesza and Taskar, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to machine learning literature.

claim: DPPs naturally capture inductive biases in human inference in word-learning and reasoning tasks.
source: Recent work in computational cognitive science has shown DPPs naturally capture inductive biases in human inference, such as some word-learning and reasoning tasks (e.g., one noun should only refer to one object) while also serving as an eﬃcient memory code (Webb et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Orthogonal coding has been proposed to be characteristic of representations in mammalian hippocampus and integral for episodic memory.
source: DPPs also provide a formal objective for the type of orthogonal coding that has been proposed to be characteristic of representations in mammalian hippocampus, and integral for episodic memory (McClelland et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to neuroscience literature.

claim: Grid cell code is implemented in the entorhinal cortex, one synapse upstream of the hippocampus.
source: Thus, using the DPP objective to govern attention over the grid cell code, known to be implemented in the entorhinal cortex (Hafting et al., 2005; Barry et al., 2007; Stensola et al., 2012; Giocomo et al., 2011; Brandon et al., 2011) (one synapse upstream of the hippocampus), aligns with the function and organization of cognitive and neural systems underlying the capability for abstraction.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to neuroscience literature.

claim: The network was trained on 80% of all sets of points in the training range, with 20% held out as the validation set.
source: The network was trained on 80% of all such sets of points in the training range, with 20% held out as the validation set.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: The total number of discrete frequencies in the entorhinal cortex has been estimated to be between 8 and 12.
source: Empirically, it has been estimated to be between 8 and 12 (Moser et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to empirical neuroscience work.

claim: Higher-frequency grid cell embeddings exhibit greater variance over the training data than lower-frequency embeddings.
source: We ﬁnd that grid cell embeddings corresponding to the higher spatial frequency grid cells exhibit greater variance over the training data than the lower-frequency embeddings, while at the same time the correlations among those grid cell embeddings are lower than the correlations among the lower-frequency grid cell embeddings.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from the experiments.

claim: Correlations among higher-frequency grid cell embeddings are lower than correlations among lower-frequency grid cell embeddings.
source: We ﬁnd that grid cell embeddings corresponding to the higher spatial frequency grid cells exhibit greater variance over the training data than the lower-frequency embeddings, while at the same time the correlations among those grid cell embeddings are lower than the correlations among the lower-frequency grid cell embeddings.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from the experiments.

claim: The determinant of the covariance matrix of grid cell embeddings is maximized when the variances are high and the correlation among embeddings is low.
source: The determinant of the covariance matrix of the grid cell embeddings is maximized when the variances of the grid cell embeddings are high (they are 'expressive') and the correlation among the grid cell embeddings is low (they 'cover the representational space').
evidence: This is based on mathematical properties of determinants and covariance matrices.

claim: Higher-frequency grid cell embeddings more efficiently cover the representational space of the training data.
source: As a result, the higher-frequency grid cell embeddings more eﬃciently cover the representational space of the training data, allowing them to eﬃciently capture the same relational structure across training and test distributions which is required for OOD generalization.
evidence: This is inferred from the mathematical properties and empirical observations.

claim: DPP-A achieves nearly perfect accuracy on all test regions for the analogy task using an LSTM inference module.
source: DPP-A (shown in blue) achieves nearly perfect accuracy on all of the test regions, considerably outperforming the other models.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3 showing experimental results.

claim: Using all grid cell code with no DPP-A led to the worst OOD generalization performance for translation in the analogy task.
source: For the case of translation, using all the grid cell code with no DPP-A (shown in purple) led to the worst OOD generalization performance, overﬁtting on the training set.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 experimental results.

claim: DPP-A substantially outperformed all other models for scaling in the analogy task, with a nearly 70% improvement in average test accuracy.
source: For the case of scaling, locked dropout and L1 regularization performed slightly better than TCN, achieving marginally higher test accuracy, but DPP-A still substantially outperformed all other models, with a nearly 70% improvement in average test accuracy.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3 showing experimental results.

claim: With no DPP-A, the transformer did poorly on analogies on the test regions.
source: With no explicit attention (no DPP-A) over the grid cell code (shown in orange), the transformer did poorly on the analogies on the test regions.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 experimental results.

claim: Simply using a more sophisticated architecture with standard forms of attention is not sufficient to enable OOD generalization based on grid cell code.
source: This suggests that simply using a more sophisticated architecture with standard forms of attention is not suﬃcient to enable OOD generalization based on the grid cell code.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results with transformers.

claim: With DPP-A, the OOD generalization performance of the transformer is nearly perfect for both translation and scaling on the analogy task.
source: With DPP-A (shown in blue), the OOD generalization performance of the transformer is nearly perfect for both translation and scaling.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4 showing experimental results.

claim: Grid cell code coupled with DPP-A can be exploited for OOD generalization effectively by different architectures.
source: These results also demonstrate that grid cell code coupled with DPP-A can be exploited for OOD generalization eﬀectively by diﬀerent architectures.
evidence: This is inferred from results with both LSTM and transformer architectures.

claim: DPP-A achieves higher accuracy for addition than multiplication on the test regions in the arithmetic task.
source: DPP-A achieves higher accuracy for addition than multiplication on the test regions.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 experimental results.

claim: DPP-A achieves nearly perfect OOD generalization for addition in the arithmetic task.
source: However, in both cases DPP-A signiﬁcantly outperforms the other models, achieving nearly perfect OOD generalization for addition, and 65% accuracy for multiplication, compared with under 20% accuracy for all the other models.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5 showing experimental results.

claim: DPP-A achieves 65% accuracy for multiplication in the arithmetic task, compared with under 20% accuracy for all other models.
source: However, in both cases DPP-A signiﬁcantly outperforms the other models, achieving nearly perfect OOD generalization for addition, and 65% accuracy for multiplication, compared with under 20% accuracy for all the other models.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5 showing experimental results.

claim: Grid cell embeddings obtained after the first step in Algorithm 1 are not able to fully preserve the relational structure for multiplication problems on the test regions.
source: We found that grid cell embeddings obtained after the ﬁrst step in Algorithm 1 are not able to fully preserve the relational structure for multiplication problems on the test regions (more details in Appendix 1: 'Why is OOD generalization performance worse for the multiplication task?'), but still it aﬀords superior capacity for OOD generalization than any of the other models.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from the experiments.

claim: With no DPP-A, the transformer achieved around 20–30% accuracy on addition and multiplication on the test regions.
source: With no DPP-A over the grid cell code the transformer did poorly on addition and multiplication on the test regions, achieving around 20–30% accuracy.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 experimental results.

claim: With DPP-A, the transformer's OOD generalization performance is nearly perfect for addition in the arithmetic task.
source: With DPP-A, the OOD generalization performance of the transformer shows a pattern similar to that for LSTM: it is nearly perfect for addition
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6 showing experimental results.

claim: With DPP-A, the transformer shows approximately 40% better performance than without DPP-A on multiplication.
source: and, though not as good on multiplication, nevertheless shows approximately 40% better performance than the transformer multiplication.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6 showing experimental results.

claim: The average accuracy on test regions for translation and scaling using smoothed one-hots passed through an encoder is nearly 30% better than simple one-hot embeddings passed through an encoder.
source: The average accuracy on the test regions for translation and scaling using smoothed one-hots passed through an encoder (shown in green) is nearly 30% better than simple one-hot embeddings passed through an encoder (shown in orange), but both still achieve signiﬁcantly lower test accuracy than grid cell code which support perfect OOD generalization.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7 showing ablation study results.

claim: Both one-hot and smoothed one-hot embeddings achieve significantly lower test accuracy than grid cell code.
source: The average accuracy on the test regions for translation and scaling using smoothed one-hots passed through an encoder (shown in green) is nearly 30% better than simple one-hot embeddings passed through an encoder (shown in orange), but both still achieve signiﬁcantly lower test accuracy than grid cell code which support perfect OOD generalization.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7 showing ablation study results.

claim: For translation, the average accuracy over test regions using grid cell code is nearly 25% more compared to other embeddings.
source: For translation (left), the average accuracy over the test regions using grid cell code (shown in blue) is nearly 25% more compared to other embeddings, which all yield performance near chance (∼15%).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 8 showing ablation study results.

claim: Grid cell code and standard error-driven learning alone are insufficient to promote OOD generalization.
source: However, despite their intrinsic structure, we ﬁnd that grid cell code and standard error-driven learning alone are insuﬃcient to promote OOD generalization, and standard approaches for preventing overﬁtting oﬀer only modest gains.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental results comparing different methods.

claim: Standard approaches for preventing overfitting offer only modest gains in OOD generalization.
source: However, despite their intrinsic structure, we ﬁnd that grid cell code and standard error-driven learning alone are insuﬃcient to promote OOD generalization, and standard approaches for preventing overﬁtting oﬀer only modest gains.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental comparisons with dropout and L1 regularization.

claim: The combination of grid cell code and DPP-A promotes OOD generalization across both translation and scale when incorporated into LSTM and transformer architectures.
source: This is addressed by the second component, using DPP-A to implement attentional regularization over the grid cell code. DPP-A allows only a relevant and diverse subset of cells to inﬂuence downstream computation in the inference module using the statistics of the training data. For proof of concept, we started with two challenging cognitive tasks (analogy and arithmetic), and showed that the combination of grid cell code and DPP-A promotes OOD generalization across both translation and scale when incorporated into common architectures (LSTM and transformer).
evidence: This is the main finding demonstrated through experiments.

claim: The DPP-A attentional mechanism is different from the attentional mechanism in the transformer module.
source: It is worth noting that the DPP-A attentional mechanism is diﬀerent from the attentional mechanism in the transformer module, and both are needed for strong OOD generalization in the case of transformers.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing both mechanisms are necessary.

claim: Use of standard self-attention in transformers over inputs in place of DPP-A would lead to weightings of grid cell embeddings over all frequencies and phases.
source: Use of the standard self-attention mechanism in transformers over the inputs (i.e., A, B, C, and D for the analogy task) in place of DPP-A would lead to weightings of grid cell embeddings over all frequencies and phases.
evidence: This is inferred from understanding of how transformer attention works.

claim: The objective function for DPP-A selectively assigns the greatest weight to all grid cell embeddings of the frequency for which the determinant of the covariance matrix is greatest.
source: The objective function for the DPP-A represents an inductive bias, that selectively assigns the greatest weight to all grid cell embeddings (i.e., for all phases) of the frequency for which the determinant of the covariance matrix is greatest computed over the training space.
evidence: This describes how the DPP-A mechanism works based on its mathematical formulation.

claim: Grid cell code can be derived using standard analytical techniques for dimensionality reduction.
source: A body of recent computational work has shown that representations similar to grid cells can be derived using standard analytical techniques for dimensionality reduction (Dordek et al., 2016; Stachenfeld et al., 2017), as well as from error-driven learning paradigms (Cueva and Wei, 2018; Banino et al., 2018; Whittington et al., 2020; Sorscher et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior computational work.

claim: Grid cells emerge in networks trained to generalize to novel location/object combinations and support transitive inference.
source: Previous work has also shown that grid cells emerge in networks trained to generalize to novel location/object combinations, and support transitive inference (Whittington et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: DPPs have been used for supervised video summarization.
source: In the ﬁeld of machine learning, DPPs have been used for supervised video summarization (Gong et al., 2014), diverse recommendations (Chen et al., 2018), selecting a subset of diverse neurons to prune a neural network without hurting performance (Mariet and Sra, 2015), and diverse minibatch attention for stochastic gradient descent (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to machine learning literature.

claim: DPPs have not previously been combined with grid cell code for OOD generalization.
source: To our knowledge, however, DPPs have not previously been combined with the grid cell code that we employ here, and have not been used to enable OOD generalization.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current work.

claim: Weight decay is a commonly employed technique to prevent deep learning systems from overfitting.
source: Various approaches have been proposed to prevent deep learning systems from overﬁtting, and enable them to generalize. A commonly employed technique is weight decay (Krogh and Hertz, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to machine learning literature.

claim: Dropout is a regularization technique which reduces overfitting by randomly zeroing units from the neural network during training.
source: Srivastava et al., 2014 proposed dropout, a regularization technique which reduces overﬁtting by randomly zeroing units from the neural network during training.
evidence: Supported by citation to machine learning literature.

claim: The prefrontal cortex encodes and actively maintains abstract information needed for task performance such as rules and relations.
source: In particular, the role of the prefrontal cortex in the encoding and active maintenance of abstract information needed for task performance (such as rules and relations) has often been modeled using gated recurrent networks, such as LSTMs (Frank et al., 2001; Braver and Cohen, 2000)
evidence: Supported by citations to neuroscience literature.

claim: The posterior parietal cortex supports 'maps' that may provide an important substrate for computing complex relations.
source: and the posterior parietal cortex has long been known to support 'maps' that may provide an important substrate for computing complex relations (Summerfield et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to neuroscience literature.

claim: The model predicts that high-frequency grid cells should increase their firing rate more than low-frequency cells when individuals are exposed to a task requiring consistent exposure to a subregion.
source: This could be tested experimentally by exposing individuals (e.g., rodents or humans) to a task that requires consistent exposure to a subregion, and evaluating the distribution of activity over the grid cells. Our model predicts that high-frequency grid cells should increase their ﬁring rate more than low-frequency cells, since the high-frequency grid cells maximize the determinant of the covariance matrix of the grid cell embeddings.
evidence: This is a testable prediction derived from the model.

claim: Bozkurt et al., 2022 proposed a biologically plausible neural network algorithm using a weighted similarity matrix approach to implement a determinant maximization criterion.
source: In that regard, Bozkurt et al., 2022 recently proposed a biologically plausible neural network algorithm using a weighted similarity matrix approach to implement a determinant maximization criterion, which is the core idea underlying the objective function we use for DPP-A (Equation 6), suggesting that the DPP-A mechanism we describe may also be biologically plausible.
evidence: Supported by citation to recent work on biological plausibility.

claim: Frankland and Cohen, 2020 suggested that the use of DPPs may help explain a mutual exclusivity bias observed in human word learning and reasoning.
source: It is also worth noting that Frankland and Cohen, 2020 have suggested that the use of DPPs may also help explain a mutual exclusivity bias observed in human word learning and reasoning.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The Tolman-Eichenbaum Machine (TEM) model suggests that grid cells in the medial entorhinal may form a basis set that captures structural knowledge for nonlinear spaces.
source: The Tolman-Eichenbaum Machine (TEM) model (Whittington et al., 2020) suggests that grid cells in the medial entorhinal may form a basis set that captures structural knowledge for such nonlinear spaces, such as social hierarchies and transitive inference when formalized as a connected graph.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Eigen decomposition of the successor representation provides an abstract structured representation of a space that is analogous to grid cell code.
source: Another would be to use eigen decomposition of the successor representation (Dayan, 1993), a learnable predictive representation of possible future states that has been shown by Stachenfeld et al., 2017 to provide an abstract structured representation of a space that is analogous to the grid cell code.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.
